newsitem.title: UK: New financial watchdog to take banks in H1 1998.
newsitem.headline: New financial watchdog to take banks in H1 1998.

text.p: Britain's new and enlarged financial watchdog, currently known as Super-SIB, will take over responsibility for supervision of the banking industry in the first half of 1998, according to proposals published on Thursday.

In a report to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, outgoing Securities and Investments Board (SIB) chairman Sir Andrew Large said the transfer of the Bank of England's responsibilities meant the plan to create a single regulator was getting off to a quick start.

The second phase of the plan will see staff of the current self-regulatory organisations (SROs), which will continue as the legal regulators until complete integration in late 1999 or early 2000, transferring to the new regulator and being employed by it.
The current nine separate bodies cover banking; insurance; building societies; the investment management industry; retail investments; and securities and futures trading.

New SIB chief Howard Davies, in his last day as deputy governor of the Bank of England, paid tribute to Large's work. "All nine bodies (SROs) are committed, at the highest level, to ensuring that the transition is as smooth and efficient as possible."

The report outlines a draft structure including Authorisation; Supervision; and Policy Formulation departments and suggests ways of ensuring greater accountability including an external appeals system, a dedicated quality control unit and more appearances by officials before the Treasury Select Committee.
The process of integrating regulation, including for the first time the supervision and surveillance of banks, was put forward by Brown in May.

The Bank of England Bill, integrating the Bank's supervisory functions with the SIB, will be presented to Parliament in the autumn. This will be followed by a draft bill to bring about full integration which will be published in the summer of 1998.
Before then, a process of extensive consultation will continue with questions including those of funding arrangements, compensation, ombudsman schemes and practitioner and consumer involvement.
The report recognises that the transition will be a "considerable challenge" and that a key aspect will be to maintain standards during the integration.
